This pattern indicates retrieval of practiced conjunctions with intrusions, which argues against the compositional account. Very slow novel RTs and accuracy well above what dominant retrieval would give in motor-differs tasks mildly favour composition being the main route (dual-route), but this is not decisive.

text:
**The results rule out a purely compositional account (A). They do not clearly separate conjunctive (B) from dual-route (C).**

### Evidence against A (compositional)

- **Share-2 tasks are faster but less accurate than share-1 tasks.** RT is 1599 vs 1783 ms, but accuracy is 66.0% vs 72.5% (p = .028). If participants only reconfigured the closest practiced task, fewer rules to change should mean both faster *and* more accurate responses. A speed–accuracy split tied to overlap is what you expect when a similar practiced task is retrieved and its responses intrude.
- **The breakdown by which rule differs fits intrusions.**
  - When the motor rule differs, accuracy is 54.9%. Here the retrieved task's button mapping is always wrong, so any intrusion becomes an error.
  - When the logic rule differs, accuracy is 63.2%. Different logic rules agree on some stimulus configurations, so some intrusions still give correct responses.
  - When the sensory rule differs, accuracy is 72.6% and RT is fastest.

  A compositional account has no natural reason why the identity of the changed rule should produce this ordering, or why a near-match would hurt accuracy.

### Why B vs C cannot be decided from these data

- Both accounts predict practiced conjunctions intruding on high-overlap novel tasks. They differ in two places:
  - **How dominant retrieval is.** B says it dominates; C says composition dominates, with occasional retrieval.
  - **Whether new conjunctions persist or decay.** B says they persist; C says they decay over intervening mini-blocks.
- **Dominance hints slightly towards C:**
  - Novel RTs are very slow (≈1700 ms, more than double practiced RT). That suggests most correct trials are composed rather than retrieved.
  - If retrieval dominated, motor-differs tasks should be near or below chance, because every intrusion there is wrong. 54.9% instead implies intrusions on only a minority of trials.
  - Against that, overall novel accuracy (68%) is low everywhere, so composition itself may simply be error-prone. That weakens the inference.
- **Persistence vs decay is the decisive contrast.** All novel-task results here are first presentations, so the data say nothing about it.

### Next step

1. **Error-type analysis.** For each novel-task error, check whether the response matches what the most-overlapping practiced task would have produced. Also check whether those errors are fast compared with correct responses. Fast, task-matching errors indicate retrieval; their frequency gauges how dominant retrieval is.
2. **Repeat-performance analysis.** Compare a novel task's second performance with its first, as a function of the number of intervening mini-blocks.
   - Under B, the benefit persists regardless of the gap.
   - Under C, the benefit decays as the gap grows.
   - Under A, any gain is only general practice, matched by first-time novel tasks at the same point in the session.

prompt:
# Interpret a cognitive experiment

Below is the method and results summary of an experiment on rapid instructed task learning. Three accounts of how participants perform novel tasks are under consideration. Exactly one of them describes these participants.

**(A) Compositional.** Participants perform novel tasks by reusing the practiced rules as separable parts: they reconfigure the practiced task set that shares the most rules with the novel task, changing the rules that differ. They do not rely on practiced conjunctive (whole-task) representations for novel tasks. Repeating a novel task only adds general practice; no new whole-task representation is formed.

**(B) Conjunctive.** Performance relies mainly on conjunctive (whole-task) representations formed during practice. A novel task tends to retrieve the practiced conjunction that shares the most rules with it: this is fast, but the retrieved task's responses intrude where the two tasks differ. Composing a novel task from its rules is possible but slow. Once a novel task has been performed, it is stored as a new conjunction that persists across the session.

**(C) Dual-route with compilation.** Participants mostly compose novel tasks from rules, but practiced conjunctions are sometimes retrieved and compete (with occasional intrusions). A novel task that has been performed is compiled into a new conjunction, but this new representation decays over intervening mini-blocks.

---

## Method (summary)

32 participants performed the Concrete Permuted Rule Operations (C-PRO) paradigm. Each task combines one logic rule (BOTH, NOT BOTH, EITHER, NEITHER), one sensory rule (RED, VERTICAL, HIGH PITCH, CONSTANT TONE), and one motor rule (LEFT INDEX, LEFT MIDDLE, RIGHT INDEX, RIGHT MIDDLE); 64 tasks in total. On each trial two audiovisual stimuli are presented; the logic rule is applied to whether each stimulus has the sensory feature, and the motor rule maps the result to a button (for example, LEFT INDEX: true -> left index finger, false -> left middle finger). Tasks are presented in mini-blocks: an instruction screen, then 3 trials, with speeded responses.

**Practice phase.** Four tasks covering all 12 rules (each rule in exactly one practiced task), practiced over 6 blocks:
- BOTH / HIGH PITCH / LEFT INDEX
- NEITHER / VERTICAL / RIGHT INDEX
- EITHER / CONSTANT TONE / LEFT MIDDLE
- NOT BOTH / RED / RIGHT MIDDLE

**Test phase.** The 4 practiced tasks (2 mini-blocks each) and 18 novel tasks. Every novel task combines practiced rules. Unless noted, novel-task results refer to the first time each novel task was performed.

RT is the mean of correct trials. SE is the standard error across participants.

## Results

**Practice.** RT and accuracy for the practiced tasks over the practice blocks:

| Block | RT | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1459 ms (SE 39) | 72.6% (SE 1.1) |
| 2 | 1016 ms (SE 30) | 84.2% (SE 0.9) |
| 3 | 898 ms (SE 27) | 86.8% (SE 0.9) |
| 4 | 876 ms (SE 26) | 88.1% (SE 0.9) |
| 5 | 847 ms (SE 25) | 89.4% (SE 0.8) |
| 6 | 830 ms (SE 25) | 90.0% (SE 1.0) |

**Test: practiced vs. novel tasks.**

| Condition | RT | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| Practiced tasks | 786 ms (SE 22) | 92.1% (SE 1.1) |
| Novel tasks | 1705 ms (SE 40) | 68.0% (SE 1.4) |

Novel vs. practiced tasks, paired t-tests: RT t(31) = 20.21, p < .001; accuracy t(31) = -14.51, p < .001.

**Novel tasks by overlap with the practice set.** Each novel task shares either 2 rules or 1 rule with its most similar practiced task (9 and 9 novel tasks). For tasks sharing 2 rules, the table also splits by which rule type differs from that practiced task.

| Novel tasks | RT | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| Share 2 rules | 1599 ms (SE 34) | 66.0% (SE 2.3) |
| Share 1 rule | 1783 ms (SE 41) | 72.5% (SE 1.9) |
| Share 2, logic rule differs | 1722 ms (SE 45) | 63.2% (SE 2.5) |
| Share 2, sensory rule differs | 1441 ms (SE 33) | 72.6% (SE 3.2) |
| Share 2, motor rule differs | 1703 ms (SE 51) | 54.9% (SE 3.8) |

Share 2 vs. share 1 rule, paired t-tests: RT t(31) = -8.86, p < .001; accuracy t(31) = -2.31, p = .028.

---

## Your judgment

Which account do these results support, and how strongly? Reason as you like, then end with one JSON object: {"account": "compositional" | "conjunctive" | "dual-route" | "cannot_tell", "probabilities": {"compositional": p, "conjunctive": p, "dual-route": p}, "key_evidence": "...", "alternative_readings": "...", "next_step": "the analysis or experiment you would run next"}. The probabilities are your probabilities that each account is the true one; they should sum to 1. Use "cannot_tell" if the results do not favour one account clearly.
